title: Answering Mormonism on the Trinity

keyTerms.d: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints uses the word “Godhead” and confesses the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost — which can sound Trinitarian, and is not. Its own Gospel Topics entry describes them as “three separate beings” who are “one in purpose,” with the Father and Son possessing “tangible bodies of flesh and bones” and the Holy Ghost “a personage of spirit.” A shared word, not a shared belief.

The conviction that God was once a man who progressed to godhood, and that the faithful may follow the same path. Its most famous summary is the couplet composed by Lorenzo Snow around 1840: “As man now is, God once was: As God now is, man may be.” (Snow’s recorded wording is “may be”; it is also widely quoted “may become.”)

Joseph Smith’s funeral sermon of April 1844, the sharpest statement of the doctrine: “God himself was once as we are now, and is an exalted man, and sits enthroned in yonder heavens,” and, to the living, “you have got to learn how to be Gods yourselves…the same as all Gods have done before you.” It is the claim with no patristic parallel — the heart of the dispute.

A corollary of exaltation: the Book of Abraham narrates creation in the plural — “they, that is the Gods, organized and formed the heavens and the earth” (Abraham 4:1). Critics describe the result as a form of social tritheism tending toward henotheism; this is a critic’s characterization, and LDS thinkers contest it, preferring to speak of one Godhead united in purpose and will.

The faith shared by Catholics, the Eastern Orthodox, and the historic Protestant traditions: there is one God — numerically one divine being, one undivided essence — who exists eternally as three coequal, coeternal persons. The persons are really distinct (the Father is not the Son), but they are not three beings; they share, wholly and without division, the one being of God.

Scripture and the fathers really do speak of believers becoming “partakers of the divine nature” (2 Peter 1:4) — glorified creatures drawn by grace into the life of God. But the believer is deified as a creature who never crosses into being God by nature; we are made “partakers,” not partners of the same species. The Creator/creature line is never crossed — which is exactly where this parts from the LDS claim that humans become Gods of the same kind.

The decisive biblical material, making a sweeping claim about reality, not merely about whom Israel should worship: “Before me no god was formed, nor shall there be any after me” (43:10); “I know not any” other God (44:8). The idiom is fenced on every side — the origination verb “formed,” sole creation “by myself” (44:24), and universal address “all the ends of the earth” (45:22).

“I the LORD do not change” (Malachi 3:6); “from everlasting to everlasting you are God” (Psalm 90:2); “God is not man, that he should … change his mind” (Numbers 23:19). He did not become God, and there was never a God before him. A God who became God is, by the Bible’s own definition — and by the logic of ultimate explanation — not God at all.

derive.q: Latter-day Saints and Nicene Christians both say “Godhead” and both name Father, Son, and Holy Ghost. So the agreement between them is…?
derive.ans: verbal only — the disagreement is real and theological
derive.why: To an outsider the shared words can sound Trinitarian, and Latter-day Saints are the first to say they are not. Both sides agree they disagree, and the LDS Church openly distinguishes its teaching from the creeds. The question is narrow and sharp: is God one being or several?

derive.q: If God the Father was once a man who progressed to deity, then before him there was…?
derive.ans: a prior god — a predecessor, and a time when he was not God
derive.why: The King Follett teaching (“the same as all Gods have done before you”) gives no stopping point for the chain. But “before me no god was formed” uses a verb of origination and excludes precisely a God who existed prior to Yahweh — the predecessor-deity that eternal progression requires.

derive.q: Isaiah says no god was “formed” before YHWH, “nor shall there be any after.” Which two LDS moves does one sentence foreclose?
derive.ans: both — no god before (progression) and no gods after (exaltation)
derive.why: “Before me no god was formed” rules out the predecessor-deity progression needs; “nor shall there be any after me” excludes the exalted gods that exaltation promises. “I know not any” (44:8) is the strongest possible denial that any rival exists, in every direction of time.

derive.q: Three figures at the baptism, the Son praying in Gethsemane, Stephen seeing two figures side by side. So what do the scenes prove — and what can they not settle?
derive.ans: they prove distinction; they cannot settle essence
derive.why: The scenes prove distinction, which the Trinity affirms every bit as firmly as Mormonism does — they refute modalism, not Trinitarianism. Three persons acting distinctly is equally compatible with three beings and with three persons of one being; to decide between those you must read the scenes together with the oneness statements.

derive.q: Grant that Isaiah and immutability tell against the LDS picture. Does that, by itself, prove the Trinity?
derive.ans: no — it shows the LDS alternative does not hold
derive.why: This argument does not by itself prove the Trinity; it shows the LDS alternative cannot be squared with Isaiah’s monotheism or the immutability of God. The positive case — one God, eternally Father, Son and Holy Spirit — rests on its own scriptural and rational supports.

honestState.p1: The descriptive claims are not in dispute: LDS theology really does teach three separate divine beings, a Father with a physical body, eternal progression, and a plurality of gods — this is the Church’s own self-description, not a hostile caricature (Gospel Topics; D&C 130:22; the King Follett discourse; the 2014 essay “Becoming Like God”). The decisive weight sits on Isaiah’s monotheism oracles and the immutability and spirituality of God, which are strong. What the argument does NOT do is prove the Trinity by itself, or settle every disputed verse — the exegesis of Psalm 82 and John 17 remains a live conversation.
honestState.fairness: A charitable treatment lets the best Latter-day Saint reading stand at full height first: serious LDS thinkers offer their own readings of Psalm 82, John 17, and the narrative scenes, and they contest the “tritheism” and “henotheism” labels as importing categories foreign to their own self-understanding. And the Christian owes a concession of his own — as the philosopher Dale Tuggy notes in the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, the “social” family of Trinitarian models shows that the line between a robust distinction of persons and tritheism is itself philosophically delicate, a point pressed against Trinitarians as well.
honestState.verdict: The honest verdict is not that the LDS position is absurd, but that it cannot be squared with Isaiah’s monotheism or with the immutability of God — and that, on its own deepest commitment, a God who progressed cannot be the uncreated ground of all things. The LDS doctrine of the Godhead is not a variant within the Trinity debate but a departure from the biblical monotheism the Trinity was formulated to protect: not the Trinity, and not the one God the Bible reveals — a shared name, a different God, and so a different Jesus. It establishes nothing about the sincerity, the morality, or the devotion of the Latter-day Saints who hold it; many plainly are sincere and devout.

order: LDS theology teaches that the Father, Son and Spirit are three separate beings, one in purpose — and that God the Father is an exalted man, one deity in an eternal chain of progression.
The Bible’s monotheism forecloses both moves categorically: before YHWH no god was formed, nor shall there be any after; he is God “from everlasting to everlasting” and does not change.

Therefore the LDS Godhead stands outside biblical monotheism — not the Trinity and not the one God the Bible reveals, a shared name, a different God, and so a different Jesus; this shows the LDS alternative does not hold, while the historic faith rests on its own scriptural case.

cards.q: State Premise 1 — and its precision check.
cards.a: LDS theology teaches the Father, Son and Spirit are three separate beings, one in purpose, and that the Father is an exalted man — one deity in an eternal chain of progression. Precision: this is a description, drawn from the Church’s own canon and sources, not a hostile caricature; the question is not whether Mormons are sincere or devout — many plainly are — but whether God is one being or several.

cards.q: State Premise 2 — and its precision check.
cards.a: The Bible’s monotheism forecloses both moves: no god was formed before YHWH, none after; he is God from everlasting and does not change. Precision: this does not by itself prove the Trinity, nor settle every disputed verse (Psalm 82, John 17 remain a live conversation); it shows the LDS alternative does not hold.

cards.q: What does the conclusion reach — and not reach?
cards.a: It reaches that the LDS Godhead is not a variant within the Trinity debate but a departure from biblical monotheism — not the Trinity and not the one God the Bible reveals, a shared name, a different God, and so a different Jesus. It does not reach a proof of the Trinity, and it says nothing about the sincerity, morality, or devotion of Latter-day Saints.

cards.q: State the LDS Godhead doctrine fairly.
cards.a: Three separate beings, one in purpose; the Father an exalted man with a body of flesh and bone (D&C 130:22); deity achieved by progression — “as God now is, man may be.” This is the Church’s own self-description, not a caricature.

Isaiah 43:10 — no god FORMED before me, none after; 44:8 — “I know not any”; 44:24 — created ALONE; Psalm 90:2 — from everlasting to everlasting YOU ARE God. No prior gods, no future gods, no becoming.

cards.q: Reply to: “Ye are gods” — Psalm 82, quoted by Jesus himself in John 10.
cards.a: Read Psalm 82 to its end: the “gods” are condemned to DIE like men (82:7) — a demotion scene, the worst possible proof-text for exaltation. Jesus’ use in John 10 is an a-fortiori argument about a word’s flexibility, made while claiming something categorically higher (“I and the Father are one”) — which is why they again sought to arrest him (10:39).

cards.q: Reply to: the early fathers taught deification too (Athanasius).
cards.a: Patristic theosis and LDS exaltation share a word and almost nothing else. Athanasius, in the very treatise where he speaks of our becoming “god,” insists on the absolute Creator/creature divide: believers are deified BY GRACE as glorified creatures who never cross into being God by nature — “partakers,” not partners of the same species — and no father ever taught that God the Father was once a man. The fathers’ doctrine requires the very line the King Follett sermon erases.

cards.q: What does the Book of Mormon itself say?
cards.a: Alma 11:28–29 — “Is there more than one God? … No.” Moroni 8:18 — God “unchangeable from all eternity.” It knows nothing of a God once a man or a plurality of gods; those are products of the later Nauvoo period. (It is no ally of the Trinity either — Alma 11:38–39 calls the Son “the very Eternal Father.”) Press it gently as a question: the later sermon, or the earlier scripture?

cards.q: The hardest objection — the narrative scenes: what do they prove, and what can’t they settle?
cards.a: They prove DISTINCTION, which the Trinity affirms as firmly as Mormonism does (the baptism and Gethsemane refute modalism, not Trinitarianism). They cannot settle ESSENCE — three persons acting distinctly fits both three beings and three persons of one being — so you read them WITH the oneness statements: the LORD is one; the Word was God; one Name (singular) at baptism.

cards.q: Reply to: Isaiah is anti-idol rhetoric, not a metaphysical census.
cards.a: The polemical setting is real, but the language is engineered to outrun the loophole: not “no god for you” but none FORMED — a verb of origins — and “I know not any” (44:8), addressed to “all the ends of the earth” (45:22). The Babylon parallel (47:8) tells against the objection — Isaiah fences his claim with origins, sole creation and universal address, which is exactly what Babylon’s boast lacks.

cards.q: Reply to: an eternal chain of gods is no stranger than your eternal uncaused God.
cards.a: The two are not symmetrical. An infinite regress of progressing gods grounds nothing — matter, law and the exaltation-system itself exist eternally UNEXPLAINED, every god inside the system and none its source. One self-existent, necessary being is not one more item in such a chain; it is the terminus explanation requires — the conclusion the contingency and cosmological arguments reach independently. And Scripture votes: “before me no god was formed.”

cards.q: Does this argument condemn Mormons, or prove the Trinity?
cards.a: No to both. It says nothing about the sincerity, morality, or devotion of Latter-day Saints — many plainly are sincere and devout. And it does not by itself prove the Trinity; it locates the fault line precisely (is God one being or several; has he always been God) and shows the LDS alternative does not hold. A shared name, a different God, and so a different Jesus — offered as an invitation, with gentleness and respect.

obj.q: The texts show three beings: at the baptism the Son is in the water, the Spirit descends, the Father speaks — three, in three places, at once; in Gethsemane the Son prays to the Father; Stephen sees two figures side by side. I am simply reading what the text shows. It is the creeds that import a Greek metaphysics of “one substance” the biblical writers never used.
obj.model: This is the objection to take most seriously, and the honest reply is that the scenes prove distinction, which the Trinity affirms every bit as firmly as Mormonism does. The baptism and Gethsemane refute modalism — the idea that Father, Son, and Spirit are mere masks — not Trinitarianism; the Son prays to the Father in Gethsemane, real address to one who is really other, the incarnate Son’s human will yielded to the Father’s (Luke 22:42). What the scenes cannot do, by themselves, is settle the question of essence: three persons acting distinctly is equally compatible with three beings and with three persons of one being. To decide between those, read the scenes together with the statements — “the LORD is one” (Deuteronomy 6:4); “the Word was God” (John 1:1); the single “name” (singular) of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit at baptism (Matthew 28:19). The Trinity is the reading that keeps both the distinction and the oneness; tritheism keeps the scenes and drops the oneness texts. John 17:21–22 is sometimes pressed here — Jesus prays that believers may “be one” as he and the Father are one — but it must be completed carefully: the oneness believers are invited into is participation by grace, creatures drawn into communion, not absorbed into the divine essence; the Father-Son oneness is categorically different in kind — the Son shares in creation (John 1:3), speaks the divine “I AM” (John 8:58), and receives the worship due to God alone (John 5:23; 20:28). So 17:21 gives no purchase to a reading on which exaltation makes the faithful gods of the same kind.

obj.q: The Bible itself teaches we can become gods. Psalm 82:6 — “you are gods, sons of the Most High” — and Jesus quotes that very verse in John 10 to defend his own deity. The fathers said it too: Athanasius wrote that the Word “became man that we might be made god.” Theosis is ancient orthodoxy; Mormonism recovered what the creeds obscured.
obj.model: Concede freely: deification language is biblical, and historic Christianity has its own rich doctrine of theosis — the fathers were not embarrassed by 2 Peter 1:4. Scripture and the fathers really do speak of believers becoming “partakers of the divine nature,” glorified creatures drawn by grace into the life of God — but not the LDS claim that humans become Gods of the same kind, or that God the Father was once a man. The patristic and LDS doctrines share a word and almost nothing else. Athanasius, in the very treatise where he speaks of our becoming “god,” insists relentlessly on the absolute divide between the uncreated Creator and everything created: the believer is deified by grace, as a glorified creature who never crosses into being God by nature; we are made “partakers,” not partners of the same species. Crucially, no church father ever taught that God the Father was once a man who progressed to deity — that is the claim with no patristic parallel, and it is the heart of the King Follett doctrine. As for Psalm 82 itself, read to its end it is the worst possible proof-text: the “gods” — corrupt human judges or rebel heavenly powers — are condemned, “like men you shall die” (82:7). It is a demotion scene. And Jesus’ use of it in John 10 is an a fortiori argument about the elasticity of a word, deployed while he claims something categorically higher (“I and the Father are one,” 10:30) — which is why his hearers again sought to arrest him (10:39).

obj.q: Isaiah’s “there is no god besides me” is polemic against Babylonian idols — no carved Marduk that can save — not a metaphysical headcount ruling out exalted beings on other worlds. The same idiom is Babylon’s own boast, “I am, and there is no one besides me” (47:8), which claims no census. You are reading a worship-polemic as if it were systematic theology.
obj.model: The polemical setting is real — concede it. But the language is engineered to outrun the loophole. Isaiah does not say “no god for you”; he says none was formed, a verb about origins, ruling out a deity prior to Yahweh. He has Yahweh disclaim knowledge of any other god: “I know not any” (44:8), the strongest possible denial that any rival exists, not merely that none is worth worshiping. And he addresses the claim to “all the ends of the earth” (45:22), not to Israel alone. The Babylon parallel (47:8) actually tells against the objection: Isaiah deliberately puts Yahweh’s “there is none besides me” and Babylon’s arrogant echo of it side by side — and the whole point is that what is blasphemous self-deception in Babylon’s mouth is sober truth in Yahweh’s. And the idiom is not left to stand alone in Yahweh’s case, as it is in Babylon’s: Isaiah fences it on every side with origins (“formed,” 43:10), sole creation (44:24), and universal address (45:22) — exactly what Babylon’s boast lacks. The text is built to exclude every conceivable rival, in every direction of time.

obj.q: An eternal regression of gods is no stranger than your one eternal uncaused God. You accept one brute eternal being; we accept an eternal chain of beings. Neither is provable — so mocking ours while asserting yours is special pleading.
obj.model: The two are not symmetrical. An infinite regress of progressing gods — each exalted by a predecessor — never grounds anything: the matter, the law, and the exaltation-system itself all simply exist, eternally and unexplained, with every god a member of the system and none its ground (LDS doctrine concedes God organizes pre-existing matter rather than creating from nothing). A self-existent, necessary being is not one more contingent item in such a series; it is the terminus that any explanation of contingent things requires — the conclusion the contingency and cosmological arguments reach on independent grounds. And here Scripture and reason converge: “before me no god was formed” is exactly the denial that God is a member of any such chain. A God who became God is, by the Bible’s own definition — and by the logic of ultimate explanation — not God at all.

unseen.q: You insist “God is spirit,” but the risen Jesus has flesh and bones — “a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have” (Luke 24:39) — and he is fully God. So a divine person can have a body. Why can’t the Father have one, as Doctrine and Covenants 130:22 teaches? An embodied, glorified God is more biblical than your bodiless abstraction.
unseen.model: The risen Christ really does have flesh and bones — concede it freely, and the reason is precisely the incarnation, not a model of deity as such. The eternal Son took a complete human nature to himself without ceasing to be God, and was raised bodily (Luke 24:39); that body is his assumed humanity, the created nature he made his own, not the divine nature turned into matter. What Scripture denies is not the Son’s risen humanity but that the Father, or the divine nature as such, is embodied: “God is spirit” (John 4:24); he is the one who “alone stretched out the heavens” (Isaiah 44:24), who is “from everlasting to everlasting” (Psalm 90:2) and “does not change” (Malachi 3:6). And that is the deeper problem for the King Follett picture: an embodied Father who was once a man is a being inside the world of matter and time — exactly the predecessor-having, progressing God that “before me no god was formed” rules out. So the Son’s body is no warrant for the Father’s. The Creator/creature line is never crossed: the incarnation is God graciously taking up our nature, not evidence that deity itself is flesh — and a God who had to become God is, by the Bible’s own definition, not God at all.
